consensus_summary: Garment primarily symbolizes a person’s spiritual state or standing before God, especially righteousness/salvation (clean/white garments) versus sin/guilt (filthy garments), with secondary uses for status/office, moral character, covering/atonement, body/resurrection, and readiness.
book_summary: Garment symbolizes righteousness, specifically the righteous acts of the saints, and can be soiled by blood and sin; opposite is nakedness.
consensus_core_identification: spiritual condition/standing before God, centered on righteousness (imputed or enacted) versus unrighteousness
book_core_identification: righteousness as the righteous acts of the saints (with capacity to be soiled)
boundary_disagreement: Book restricts the primary referent to righteous acts of the saints (Rev 19:8) and soiling by sin/blood, whereas consensus admits a broader field that commonly includes imputed/Christ’s righteousness, divine covering for shame, and status/office as co-primary or closely merged readings.
rationale: Minimum cores share the same central category (righteousness as what the garment represents). The book does not replace that referent but narrows its precision and extension to ‘the righteous acts of the saints’ plus defilement, excluding or de-emphasizing the imputed-righteousness and covering-atonement emphases that consensus treats as inside the primary symbolic field. Differences are therefore boundary/precision refinements, not contradictory cores.
strongest_objection: Consensus frequently treats imputed righteousness / being clothed with Christ as equally or more central than ‘righteous acts,’ so the book’s exclusive phrasing could be read as quietly selecting one pole of an intra-consensus debate.
